 Persons with albinism demand specialised healthcare, tax-free sunscreen
Friday, November 06, 2026
 Jounalist Solomon Kaweesa addresses the media in Kampala on Friday. Photo | Godfrey Mutumba
 By  
 Shabibah Nakirigya 
What you need to know:
 They say limited access to sunscreen, protective clothing, sunglasses and specialised medical care exposes them to skin and eye complications
 People living with albinism have appealed to government to establish specialised healthcare services in public hospitals and provide essential protective products to reduce health complications associated with exposure to sunlight.
 They say limited access to sunscreen, protective clothing, sunglasses and specialised medical care exposes them to skin and eye complications, yet many cannot afford products required to protect themselves.
 Speaking to media during launch of dinner dubbed Discover Kaweesa Solomon Dinner in Kampala today Ms Faith Bwanika, secretary of Matayo Foundation, said government should integrate services for people with albinism into public health facilities, including Health Centre IVs and Mulago National Referral Hospital.

 "People living with albinism need regular medical assessments, particularly of their skin and eyes, to identify complications early and receive appropriate treatment," she said.
 Ms Bwanika said parents also have critical responsibility to support children born with condition by accepting them, protecting them from excessive sunlight and ensuring they receive proper care from early age.
 "Charity begins at home. If a parent does not support their child, how do you expect other people to support that child? Parents should understand that these children need protection from sunlight and should not be exposed to unnecessary risks," she said.
 She explained people with albinism require sunscreen lotions to protect their skin from ultraviolet radiation, sunglasses to protect their eyes and hats to shield their heads and necks from direct sunlight.
 "The rising intensity of sunlight makes these products essential rather than optional," she said, adding many people with albinism struggle to obtain them because of their cost.
 She called for specialised medical services similar to those provided to people living with HIV, arguing people with albinism should also have access to health workers familiar with their condition.
 "When a person living with HIV goes to hospital, they can access antiretroviral drugs. We also need to go to hospitals where health workers understand our condition and can ask whether we have skin problems, eye complications or need protective clothing," she said.
 She urged government to recruit dermatologists and other specialists who can examine patients, assess effects of sunlight on their skin and recommend appropriate treatment.
 Bwanika also called for government support to organisations such as Matayo Foundation, which mobilise resources and provide essential products to people living with albinism.
 Meanwhile, senior journalist Solomon Kaweesa who is spearheading fundraising dinner organising said charity aims at mobilising resources for people living with albinism and support establishment of one-stop centre where they can access assistance, share experiences and discuss challenges affecting them.
 Dinner is being organised in partnership with Matayo Twinomujuni, director of Matayo Foundation, organization which advocates for people living with albinism.
 "The initiative was inspired by an experience in 2016 when I visited a family in Jinja District with seven children living with albinism, whom I found in extremely difficult circumstances," he said.
 He added children were forced to work in gardens even during hot seasons because of their family's poverty which also contributed to their health complications.
 "I was deeply touched by their situation and decided to follow up on the family after some time. Unfortunately, I discovered that three of the children had died because of the poor conditions in which they were living," Kaweesa said.
 He said experience strengthened his determination to advocate for people living with albinism and mobilise support to improve their welfare.
 In 2021, he met Twinomujuni, who shared similar concerns, and two agreed to establish initiative to support people living with condition.Since then, they have provided some essential items, including sunscreen lotions, but Kaweesa said limited resources had prevented them from reaching significant number of beneficiaries.
 "We have tried to support these people with some of their basic needs, including sunscreen, but we cannot do it alone. We need more people to come on board because the needs are enormous," he said.
 He said their long-term goal was to establish one-stop centre where people with albinism could meet, share experiences, discuss their challenges and receive assistance.
 Kaweesa also expressed concern over government's failure to conclude discussions on proposal to remove taxes on essential products used by people living with albinism.
 He said proposal was raised during tenure of former Speaker of Parliament Rebecca Kadaga but had since stalled.
 "We realised that since then, the government has stopped discussing the matter, and no one seems to be talking about it. These are essential products that people living with albinism need to protect themselves," he said.
 Mr Twinomujuni said initiative also seeks to address social isolation and economic challenges faced by people with albinism by extending support to communities across country.
 "We intend to identify beneficiaries' abilities and equip them with practical skills to enable them to earn a living and become economically independent," he said.
 He also raised concern over abandonment of some mothers after giving birth to children with albinism, saying discrimination against condition remains challenge in some families.
 Mr Twinomujuni urged corporate organisations to provide employment and business opportunities to people with albinism, arguing they have same abilities and potential as other members of society.
 He further appealed to government to increase its support and ensure people with albinism are represented in leadership and decision-making positions so their concerns can receive greater attention.
 Charity fundraising dinner will take place on November 27, 2026, at Pope Paul Memorial Hotel in Rubaga Division, Kampala.
 Organisers have set contributions at Shs150,000 for ordinary tickets, Shs350,000 for VIP tickets and Shs3 million for a table.
